title: Coffee Ice Cream
subtitle: Espresso custard ice cream with a strong, clean coffee flavour
excerpt: A custard ice cream made with real espresso rather than instant powder, giving a sharper, cleaner coffee note. Use fresh shots and let them cool completely before adding to the custard.
sourceNotes: Coffee ice cream, often labelled caffè gelato in Italian-influenced versions, has been made in Britain since at least the mid-20th century. The use of real espresso rather than instant became the home-cook standard in the UK from the 1990s onwards as espresso machines became more common in domestic kitchens.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Press baking paper against the surface to prevent ice crystals.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The custard base can be made the day before and kept covered in the fridge before churning.

content.text: Coffee ice cream uses real espresso whisked into the custard base. It gives a clean, direct coffee flavour that instant powder cannot match. Make the custard with egg yolks, sugar, milk, and cream in the usual way. Add the espresso off the heat once the custard has thickened.

Make 2 shots of espresso (about 100ml total) and leave to cool to room temperature. Do not use instant coffee granules, they give a flat, slightly bitter flavour that lacks the complexity of fresh espresso. If you do not have an espresso machine, a moka pot produces a result close enough.

Whisk the egg yolks and caster sugar together in a large heatproof bowl until pale and slightly thickened. Combine the milk and cream in a medium saucepan and heat to just below boiling. Pour the hot cream mixture slowly onto the yolks, whisking continuously, then return to the saucepan over a low heat. Stir with a wooden spoon for 8 to 10 minutes until the custard thickens and coats the back of the spoon. Remove from the heat and stir in the cooled espresso. Pour into a clean bowl, press cling film onto the surface, and cool completely. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours.

Churn the cold custard in an ice cream maker for 25 minutes until thick and softly set. Transfer to a freezer-safe container, press baking paper against the surface, seal, and freeze for at least 6 hours or overnight.

items.symptom: Coffee flavour is weak after freezing
items.cause: Freezing mutes flavours, and espresso flavour in particular can seem fainter when cold.
items.fix: Taste the custard before churning and adjust if needed by adding a tablespoon of very strong cold espresso. The frozen version will taste slightly milder than the custard, so err on the side of a stronger custard.

items.symptom: Ice cream has a slightly grainy or icy texture
items.cause: The custard was added to the machine before it was fully chilled, or the machine bowl was not frozen sufficiently.
items.fix: The custard must be properly cold, ideally at 4°C or below, before churning. Keep it in the fridge overnight if time allows.

items.cause: The heat was too high or the stirring was interrupted.
items.fix: Strain through a fine sieve immediately. A slightly over-cooked custard that still tastes good can often be rescued by straining.

content.text: Keeps in the freezer for up to 3 months. Remove from the freezer 5 minutes before scooping.
